Here’s how this usually plays out in real-world government shutdown situations: 	-if the House votes at 7 PM ET and the bill passes, it still needs Senate approval (unless the Senate already passed the same text earlier).  -Once both chambers pass the same version, it must be signed by the President before funding legally resumes. -The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) only updates its Operating Status after the funding is officially restored - usually after the President signs the bill. -OPM typically posts that update late at night or early the next morning (ET), depending on timing.  So, in your example:  -If everything passes and the President signs the same evening (before midnight ET), OPM might update its page that night (and the market would resolve to that same calendar date). -However, in practice, it’s more common for OPM to announce the reopening the next calendar day (ET) - even if the bill passed the previous night - because the update is posted when offices prepare to reopen.

The bottleneck for this market is the OPM website. The timeline of the lifting process of the last shutdown in 2018-2019 was quite similar to the current situation. The House voted in the early evening of January 25, 2019, and the President signed the funding bill at around 9:30 PM ET. The underlying OPM website for the resolution was archived at 1:43 AM ET on January 26 and still displayed the "lapse in appropriations" notice. When the site was scraped again later that morning, at 3:28 AM ET, the notice was gone and the status had changed to "open." In my opinion, this represents a significant flaw within the market's rules, as the law takes effect the moment the President signs it. However, anyone expecting a swift process tomorrow should take this timing into account.
